lessons.title: Declare the grain before joining
lessons.summary: Prevent double counting when combining facts at different levels.

blocks.title: The mental model
blocks.body: Use the input and output grain as a contract. MAX(shipping) works in this tiny example because shipping is constant for each order; it is not a universal fix for duplicate joins.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: Joining two fact tables on a non-unique dimension key can multiply both measures.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: Where should the shipping charge live, and how would you allocate it to products?

code.source:
WITH headers(order_id, shipping) AS (VALUES (1, 10), (2, 6)),
lines(order_id, line_id, amount) AS (VALUES (1, 1, 30), (1, 2, 70), (2, 1, 50))
SELECT h.order_id, COUNT(*) AS lines, SUM(h.shipping) AS duplicated_shipping,
       MAX(h.shipping) AS order_shipping
FROM headers h JOIN lines l ON h.order_id = l.order_id
GROUP BY h.order_id ORDER BY h.order_id;

lessons.title: History with SCD type 2
lessons.summary: Match an event to the dimension version valid at event time.

blocks.title: The mental model
blocks.body: Business identity and version identity are different. A fact must link to the intended version, not merely the current city.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: BETWEEN includes both endpoints. Adjacent inclusive intervals can match the boundary event twice.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: Which city should receive the sale on exactly May 1?

code.source:
WITH dim(customer_id, city, valid_from, valid_to) AS (
 VALUES (42, 'Oslo', DATE '2026-01-01', DATE '2026-05-01'),
        (42, 'Bergen', DATE '2026-05-01', DATE '2026-09-01'),
        (42, 'Oslo', DATE '2026-09-01', DATE '9999-12-31')
), sales(customer_id, sold_at, amount) AS (
 VALUES (42, DATE '2026-04-20', 40), (42, DATE '2026-05-01', 60)
)
SELECT s.sold_at, d.city, s.amount FROM sales s JOIN dim d
 ON s.customer_id = d.customer_id
 AND s.sold_at >= d.valid_from AND s.sold_at < d.valid_to
ORDER BY s.sold_at;

lessons.title: Build SCD type 2 history
lessons.summary: Turn a change log into versions with valid_from and valid_to, open a version only on a real change, and keep one current row per key.

blocks.title: One row per version
blocks.body: A type 2 dimension keeps history: a change of a tracked attribute closes the current row and opens a new one. Each version has a surrogate key, the business key, the attributes, valid_from, valid_to (exclusive, often 9999-12-31 while current) and is_current. Facts store the surrogate key of the version valid when the event happened.

blocks.title: From a change log
blocks.body: When the source lists every change with its date, the versions come from a window function: valid_to = LEAD(changed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY changed_at), and the last version gets the open-ended date. First drop the rows whose tracked attributes did not change, or you create versions that differ only by date.

blocks.title: Change detection and NULL
blocks.body: city <> previous_city is NULL, not true, when one side is NULL, so a change to or from NULL is missed. Compare with IS DISTINCT FROM. In dbt, a snapshot keeps this history for you (dbt_valid_from, dbt_valid_to) with the timestamp or the check strategy.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: Predict how many versions customer 42 gets, and why the change log row of 2026-03-10 does not open one.

code.source:
WITH changes(customer_id, changed_at, city) AS (
  VALUES (42, DATE '2026-01-01', 'Oslo'), (42, DATE '2026-03-10', 'Oslo'),
         (42, DATE '2026-05-01', 'Bergen'), (7, DATE '2026-02-01', NULL),
         (7, DATE '2026-04-01', 'Lyon')
), real_changes AS (
  SELECT *, LAG(city) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY changed_at) AS previous_city,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY changed_at) AS n
  FROM changes
)
SELECT customer_id, city, changed_at AS valid_from,
       COALESCE(LEAD(changed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY changed_at), DATE '9999-12-31') AS valid_to,
       LEAD(changed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY changed_at) IS NULL AS is_current
FROM real_changes
WHERE n = 1 OR city IS DISTINCT FROM previous_city
ORDER BY customer_id, valid_from;

steps.title: The change log
steps.body: Customer 42 appears three times, customer 7 twice; one of 42's rows repeats the same city.

steps.title: Compare with the previous row
steps.body: LAG brings the previous city onto each row; ROW_NUMBER marks the first row of each customer.

steps.title: Keep real changes only
steps.body: WHERE runs before the window functions of the SELECT: the repeated Oslo row is gone, and NULL to Lyon counts as a change.

steps.title: Close each version
steps.body: LEAD gives the next valid_from as this version's valid_to; the last version is open-ended and current.

lessons.title: dbt tests: make assumptions fail loudly
lessons.summary: Declare unique, not_null, relationships and accepted_values tests, write singular tests as queries that return bad rows, and choose warn or error.

blocks.title: A test is a query for bad rows
blocks.body: Every dbt data test compiles to a SELECT that returns the rows breaking an assumption; it passes when that query returns no row. Generic tests are declared in YAML under a column: unique, not_null, accepted_values (with values: [...]) and relationships (to: ref('dim_customers'), field: customer_id). dbt test runs them; dbt build runs each model's tests right after the model and skips its children when a test fails.

blocks.title: Singular tests
blocks.body: A .sql file in tests/ is a singular test: write the query that returns the violations, for example the orders whose total differs from the sum of their lines. Use one for rules that span tables or need arithmetic.

blocks.title: Severity and scope
blocks.body: config: severity: warn reports a failure without failing the run; error_if and warn_if set thresholds such as ">10". where: limits a test to the rows that matter (status <> 'cancelled'). Warn on known, tolerated issues; keep keys and relationships at error.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: The example is, in plain SQL, what the four generic tests check on a small fct_orders. Predict which test returns which row.

code.source:
WITH fct_orders(order_id, customer_id, status) AS (
  VALUES (1, 10, 'placed'), (2, 11, 'shipped'), (2, 11, 'shipped'), (3, NULL, 'returned'), (4, 12, 'lost')
), dim_customers(customer_id) AS (VALUES (10), (11))
SELECT 'unique order_id' AS test, CAST(order_id AS VARCHAR) AS failing_value
FROM fct_orders GROUP BY order_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
UNION ALL
SELECT 'not_null customer_id', CAST(order_id AS VARCHAR) FROM fct_orders WHERE customer_id IS NULL
UNION ALL
SELECT 'accepted_values status', status FROM fct_orders WHERE status NOT IN ('placed', 'shipped', 'returned')
UNION ALL
SELECT 'relationships customer_id', CAST(f.customer_id AS VARCHAR)
FROM fct_orders f LEFT JOIN dim_customers d ON f.customer_id = d.customer_id
WHERE f.customer_id IS NOT NULL AND d.customer_id IS NULL;

steps.title: unique
steps.body: Group by the key and keep the groups with more than one row: order 2 appears twice.

steps.title: not_null
steps.body: Rows whose column is NULL: order 3 has no customer.

steps.title: accepted_values
steps.body: Values outside the list: "lost" is not an accepted status.

steps.title: relationships
steps.body: Child keys with no parent: customer 12 is not in dim_customers. NULL keys are left to not_null.
